definition: The remember–know procedure is a memory method that asks whether retrieval is accompanied by conscious recollection of a past event or instead by a mere feeling of knowing. It is used to distinguish recollective awareness from familiarity-like knowing when studying episodic memory.

reasons: The definition claims the procedure “asks whether retrieval is accompanied by conscious recollection … or instead by a mere feeling of knowing.” The packet does not describe the procedure as an explicit question/decision about “retrieval is accompanied by…”; it only mentions that the authors used a “Remember/Know procedure” in relation to whether episodic retrieval involves a “recollective experience” versus a “feeling of knowing.”

The definition states it is used “to distinguish recollective awareness from familiarity-like knowing.” The packet does not mention “familiarity-like” knowing or that specific distinction; it only contrasts “recollective experience” with “a feeling of knowing.”

The definition refers to “remember–know procedure” as a “memory method” and links it to “episodic memory” studying; while episodic memory is discussed, the packet does not explicitly define the remember–know procedure itself as a “memory method” with the stated purpose (distinguishing recollection vs familiarity-like knowing).
